Replying to @naomi when pricing my pieces I consider time spent making/decorating/signing/waxing/glazing/sanding/lustering/firing/invetorying. I have done time studies to help gauge the time I spend on making the pieces. I also consider materials used. I apply gold luster to almost every piece and it’s expensive and requires an additional firing which is also another expense. I also consider experience. I have been working with clay for 14 years now so I consider all of those years of working to this point in my pieces value as well. Pricing is hard! Placing a value on your art is uncomfortable. I’m just happy to be here and I’m doing my best with the knowledge I have gained so far on this journey. I don’t think there is a right answer that will work for everyone, I’m just trying to do what feels right to me! Thank you for reading! 💗💗💗💗 #wheelthrown #ceramics #sliptrailing #potterytiktok #porcelain

This piece of functional art is here to remind you that no matter how gloopy and messy life gets, there is always love and joy bursting through. 🌈💗 I am so excited to finally start sharing the first pieces from my 2026 collection! The first half of this year has been full of learning, experimenting, and pushing my work in new directions. It has also been one of the heaviest seasons of my life. While making this collection, I found myself returning again and again to the same idea: choosing hope. This piece feels like a little celebration of that. A reminder that even when things feel overwhelming, beautiful things can still emerge from the mess. Thankfully, the scary chapter my chosen family has been living through is coming to a very happy ending, and I am sitting in deep gratitude for that. Not everyone gets that outcome, and I don’t take it for granted for a second. So tell me, what makes you stay hopeful when life feels extra gloopy? #ceramicartist #dopaminedecor #glitterinlay #rainbowart #processvideo

When pulling larger amounts of clay we need to stop and think of the limitations of our material alongside the additional weight. Pulling a cylinder on 1-3lbs of clay is different from pulling a cylinder on 5+lbs of clay. This is due to the immense amount of weight that is being supported by base of our vessel. If we thin out this base too early on we risk failure due to collapse. These thin walls at the bottom of the vessel struggle to support the weight above it in conjunction with the force caused by the centrifugal force of the wheel when moving it. To resolve this issue we must begin or first pull higher up the vessel. I choose to begin at the middle with my first pull to even out this weight and force. Then move my way back down to the bottom. #harleyweiglestudio #potterytutorials

It’s been some time since I last returned to the slow, methodical business of clay testing, but this week I found myself back there again, working through a small series of black stoneware tests using a new body sent to me by Valentine Clays. The timing felt appropriate, a brief pause in the year where the workshop can become a place for looking closely rather than producing quickly. The clay is called Schwarz, a name that leaves little to the imagination, and one that was repeatedly suggested when I previously spoke about my ongoing search for a genuinely black clay body that behaved. It contains 25% grog, yet in the hands it feels unexpectedly smooth, this is explained by the minute particle size, which is extremely fine at around 0.02 mm. The result is a body that throws cleanly, trims crisply, and carries its edges with confidence whilst still retaining the structural benefits that grog can provide. There’s a reassuring density to it as you work, and a sense that it wants to hold its form rather than collapse into softness. That said, no clay arrives without its compromises. The maximum firing temperature is listed at 1240ºC, which sits some way below the cone ten firings that my work is normally pushed to. Rather than dismissing it outright, I’m more interested in seeing how it behaves when blended with higher-firing bodies, and whether its colour and strength can survive a reduction firing up to 1290ºC. Over the coming weeks I’ll be mixing, testing, and firing a range of variations, paying close attention to how the black responds, and whether the pots retain their intended geometry once they’ve passed through the kiln. As ever, the answers lie less in assumptions and more in repetition, observation, and time. Thanks very much for watching and if you’d like to see a more exploratory video that discusses the entirety of the throwing and trimming, you can find a link to longer video via the Linktree in my profile’s biography. #pottery #ceramics #clay #stoneware #handmade
